items.title: How to Turn a Slack Thread into a Tracked Task (and Get a PR Back)
items.summary: A lot of engineering work starts the same way: someone drops a message in Slack. "The export button breaks on Safari." A few replies later, someone posts a screenshot, someone else finds the cause, and everyone agrees it should be fixed. Then the thread scrolls out of view, and nothing happens. The decision was made. It just never became a task, and it definitely never became code. In this guide, I'll show how to close that gap with Sharkly.ai: turning a Slack thread into a tracked Task, handing it to a coding agent, and getting a pull request back, without the context getting lost along the way. Everything here is based on Sharkly's Slack integration docs and its integrations overview. Why Slack Threads Are Where Tasks Go to Die Slack is great for deciding things. It's bad at remembering them. A typical thread has everything a developer needs: the bug report, a screenshot, the steps to reproduce, and often the fix someone already suggested. But to turn that into work, someone has to: Open the tracker Create a ticket and copy the important parts of the thread Re-upload the screenshots Paste a link back to Slack so people know it's tracked Remember to update the thread when it's done Every one of those steps is a chance for the work to stall. And now that coding agents can pick up well-defined tasks, the cost of that handoff is even more obvious. The agent could fix the bug in minutes. The problem is getting a clear task in front of it. What you want is a single path: thread → task → agent → pull request → back to the thread. How Sharkly's Slack Integration Works Before the steps, it helps to know that Sharkly's Slack integration is really three separate connections. Each one is set up on its own, and connecting one doesn't turn on the others. Connection What it does Who sets it up Workspace connection Create Tasks from Slack with a slash command, global shortcut, or message shortcut. Adds linkbacks and link previews. Org Owners or Admins Task assistant A built-in assistant per Space. @-mention it in a thread and it reads the conversation, writes up the request, and files a Task. Any member of that Space Agent bot Gives one Sharkly Agent its own Slack app, so you can DM it or mention it in channels. The Agent's owner, or Owners and Admins For this workflow, you mainly need the first two. The Agent bot is useful for chatting with an agent directly, but the docs note that Agent bot conversations don't create Tasks automatically , so it isn't the right tool for turning a thread into tracked work. On the code side, Sharkly's GitHub integration links pull requests back to Tasks, which is how the PR finds its way home. Step by Step: From Slack Thread to Pull Request Step 1: Connect your Slack workspace An Organization Owner or Admin does this once: In Sharkly, go to Integrations → Slack . Under Connected Slack workspaces , select Connect . Complete the Slack OAuth installation. Turn on Linkbacks and Unfurls , so the thread gets a reply with the Task link and Task links expand into previews. One thing to know: a Slack workspace can only be connected to one Sharkly Organization at a time. Step 2: Bind the Task assistant to your Space This is the part that does the heavy lifting. Each Space has a built-in Task assistant, and you just need to give it a Slack app: Open Integrations and go to the Slack page. Under Task assistant , find your Space. Select Bind Slack . Pick the Runtime for the assistant. Create and install its Slack app in the same dialog. You don't need to create an Agent first. The assistant's Description and Instructions come from your admin's template, and you can override them per Space. Step 3: Turn the thread into a Task Back in that bug thread, you have two options. Option A: mention the Task assistant. Reply in the thread with something like: @TaskAssistant turn this into a task. Fix the Safari export bug from the screenshot above. The assistant reads the conversation, writes up the request, and files the Task in that Space. You don't have to copy anything. Option B: use a message shortcut. Open the message's shortcut menu and create a Task from it. You pick the Space, task type, and status. Images, videos, and other attachments you select are carried into the Task body, so the screenshot comes with it. Either way, the thread gets a linkback, so everyone can see the work is now tracked. Step 4: Keep the thread connected The docs describe Task-bound threads : when a Task is created from Slack by an agent, the thread can be bound to it. Once bound, Task comments and thread messages stay in sync, and status changes can post back to the thread. In the Task view, you'll see thread connected in #channel . You can stop the sync there at any time without deleting the Task or the Slack history. This is what stops the thread from going quiet. The people who reported the bug see progress right where they reported it. Step 5: Assign a coding agent Now the Task is a normal Sharkly Task, so you assign it the same way you'd assign a teammate. Sharkly describes Agents as "saved Agents you assign like teammates," and you can assign an Agent or a Crew directly from the Task. One setup detail matters here: the agent needs access to your code. In Sharkly, an Agent's repositories are configured on the Agent, and it runs on a Computer , which clones using that machine's SSH key, HTTPS token, or host credentials. The agent then does the work with your coding tool of choice, such as Claude Code or Codex. You can also update the Task from Slack itself. From the Slack Task card, members can change the status, priority, assignee, labels, and dates, and the changes sync back to Sharkly. Step 6: Get the pull request back The agent works on the Task in its own worktree, and its results and blockers come back as comments on the Task. According to Sharkly, a run that's waiting for human review lands in the responsible person's Inbox. To connect the code itself back to the Task, set up the GitHub integration: Install the Sharkly GitHub App. Under Link git PRs & commits to tasks , turn on Link pull requests (and optionally Link git commits ). Make sure the Task ID appears in the PR title, the PR description, or the branch name. A bare ID like ID-123 is enough. Once a pull request that includes the Task ID is opened, Sharkly links it to the Task and can post a linkback comment on the PR. Now the PR points to the Task, the Task points to the Slack thread, and the thread shows the progress. A reviewer checks the PR, merges it, and marks the Task done, which can post the status change back to the original thread. The person who reported the bug sees it fixed without asking. Tips and Things to Know A few details from the docs that are easy to miss: Merging doesn't close the Task. Words like "fixes" or "closes" in a PR have no special meaning, and merging a PR doesn't change the Task status. Someone still marks it done. Linking a PR isn't the same as code access. The GitHub App links PRs to Tasks, but it doesn't let an agent clone your repo. That comes from the Computer's credentials. Agents see the last 20 thread messages. For longer threads, the agent can page back through Slack history using the CLI, but it's better to keep the key details near the end. You can stop a run from Slack. Add the ❌ reaction to the message that started an agent run, and it stops in Sharkly too. Turn on Slack DMs for yourself. Connect your personal Slack account under Settings → Notifications → Slack to get assignments, status changes, comments, and agent activity as DMs. Only events after you connect are delivered. People outside your org can still report. Slack users who aren't Sharkly members get an external account. It takes no seat and can't sign in, but their messages still count as context. Final Thoughts Most teams don't have a shortage of decisions. They have a shortage of follow-through. The bug gets discussed, everyone agrees, and then the thread disappears. With Sharkly's Slack integration, the path from conversation to code is much shorter: Mention the Task assistant in the thread, or use a message shortcut Keep the thread bound to the Task so updates flow both ways Assign a coding agent like you'd assign a teammate Link the PR with the Task ID and review it as usual The context from Slack travels with the work, the agent gets a clear task, and the people who raised the issue see it resolved in the same thread. If you want to try it, you can get started at sharkly.ai.
items.summary_html:
A lot of engineering work starts the same way: someone drops a message in Slack.

"The export button breaks on Safari." A few replies later, someone posts a screenshot, someone else finds the cause, and everyone agrees it should be fixed. Then the thread scrolls out of view, and nothing happens.

The decision was made. It just never became a task, and it definitely never became code.

In this guide, I'll show how to close that gap with Sharkly.ai: turning a Slack thread into a tracked Task, handing it to a coding agent, and getting a pull request back, without the context getting lost along the way. Everything here is based on Sharkly's Slack integration docs and its integrations overview.

Why Slack Threads Are Where Tasks Go to Die

Slack is great for deciding things. It's bad at remembering them.

A typical thread has everything a developer needs: the bug report, a screenshot, the steps to reproduce, and often the fix someone already suggested. But to turn that into work, someone has to:

  1. Open the tracker
  2. Create a ticket and copy the important parts of the thread
  3. Re-upload the screenshots
  4. Paste a link back to Slack so people know it's tracked
  5. Remember to update the thread when it's done

Every one of those steps is a chance for the work to stall. And now that coding agents can pick up well-defined tasks, the cost of that handoff is even more obvious. The agent could fix the bug in minutes. The problem is getting a clear task in front of it.

What you want is a single path: thread → task → agent → pull request → back to the thread.

How Sharkly's Slack Integration Works

Before the steps, it helps to know that Sharkly's Slack integration is really three separate connections. Each one is set up on its own, and connecting one doesn't turn on the others.

Connection What it does Who sets it up Workspace connection Create Tasks from Slack with a slash command, global shortcut, or message shortcut. Adds linkbacks and link previews. Org Owners or Admins Task assistant A built-in assistant per Space. @-mention it in a thread and it reads the conversation, writes up the request, and files a Task. Any member of that Space Agent bot Gives one Sharkly Agent its own Slack app, so you can DM it or mention it in channels. The Agent's owner, or Owners and Admins

For this workflow, you mainly need the first two. The Agent bot is useful for chatting with an agent directly, but the docs note that Agent bot conversations don't create Tasks automatically, so it isn't the right tool for turning a thread into tracked work.

On the code side, Sharkly's GitHub integration links pull requests back to Tasks, which is how the PR finds its way home.

Step by Step: From Slack Thread to Pull Request

Step 1: Connect your Slack workspace

An Organization Owner or Admin does this once:

  1. In Sharkly, go to Integrations → Slack.
  2. Under Connected Slack workspaces, select Connect.
  3. Complete the Slack OAuth installation.
  4. Turn on Linkbacks and Unfurls, so the thread gets a reply with the Task link and Task links expand into previews.

One thing to know: a Slack workspace can only be connected to one Sharkly Organization at a time.

Step 2: Bind the Task assistant to your Space

This is the part that does the heavy lifting. Each Space has a built-in Task assistant, and you just need to give it a Slack app:

  1. Open Integrations and go to the Slack page.
  2. Under Task assistant, find your Space.
  3. Select Bind Slack.
  4. Pick the Runtime for the assistant.
  5. Create and install its Slack app in the same dialog.

You don't need to create an Agent first. The assistant's Description and Instructions come from your admin's template, and you can override them per Space.

Step 3: Turn the thread into a Task

Back in that bug thread, you have two options.

Option A: mention the Task assistant. Reply in the thread with something like:

@TaskAssistant turn this into a task. Fix the Safari export bug
from the screenshot above.

The assistant reads the conversation, writes up the request, and files the Task in that Space. You don't have to copy anything.

Option B: use a message shortcut. Open the message's shortcut menu and create a Task from it. You pick the Space, task type, and status. Images, videos, and other attachments you select are carried into the Task body, so the screenshot comes with it.

Either way, the thread gets a linkback, so everyone can see the work is now tracked.

Step 4: Keep the thread connected

The docs describe Task-bound threads: when a Task is created from Slack by an agent, the thread can be bound to it. Once bound, Task comments and thread messages stay in sync, and status changes can post back to the thread.

In the Task view, you'll see thread connected in #channel. You can stop the sync there at any time without deleting the Task or the Slack history.

This is what stops the thread from going quiet. The people who reported the bug see progress right where they reported it.

Step 5: Assign a coding agent

Now the Task is a normal Sharkly Task, so you assign it the same way you'd assign a teammate. Sharkly describes Agents as "saved Agents you assign like teammates," and you can assign an Agent or a Crew directly from the Task.

One setup detail matters here: the agent needs access to your code. In Sharkly, an Agent's repositories are configured on the Agent, and it runs on a Computer, which clones using that machine's SSH key, HTTPS token, or host credentials.

The agent then does the work with your coding tool of choice, such as Claude Code or Codex.

You can also update the Task from Slack itself. From the Slack Task card, members can change the status, priority, assignee, labels, and dates, and the changes sync back to Sharkly.

Step 6: Get the pull request back

The agent works on the Task in its own worktree, and its results and blockers come back as comments on the Task. According to Sharkly, a run that's waiting for human review lands in the responsible person's Inbox.

To connect the code itself back to the Task, set up the GitHub integration:

  1. Install the Sharkly GitHub App.
  2. Under Link git PRs & commits to tasks, turn on Link pull requests (and optionally Link git commits).
  3. Make sure the Task ID appears in the PR title, the PR description, or the branch name. A bare ID like ID-123 is enough.

Once a pull request that includes the Task ID is opened, Sharkly links it to the Task and can post a linkback comment on the PR. Now the PR points to the Task, the Task points to the Slack thread, and the thread shows the progress.

A reviewer checks the PR, merges it, and marks the Task done, which can post the status change back to the original thread. The person who reported the bug sees it fixed without asking.

Tips and Things to Know

A few details from the docs that are easy to miss:

  • Merging doesn't close the Task. Words like "fixes" or "closes" in a PR have no special meaning, and merging a PR doesn't change the Task status. Someone still marks it done.
  • Linking a PR isn't the same as code access. The GitHub App links PRs to Tasks, but it doesn't let an agent clone your repo. That comes from the Computer's credentials.
  • Agents see the last 20 thread messages. For longer threads, the agent can page back through Slack history using the CLI, but it's better to keep the key details near the end.
  • You can stop a run from Slack. Add the ❌ reaction to the message that started an agent run, and it stops in Sharkly too.
  • Turn on Slack DMs for yourself. Connect your personal Slack account under Settings → Notifications → Slack to get assignments, status changes, comments, and agent activity as DMs. Only events after you connect are delivered.
  • People outside your org can still report. Slack users who aren't Sharkly members get an external account. It takes no seat and can't sign in, but their messages still count as context.
Final Thoughts

Most teams don't have a shortage of decisions. They have a shortage of follow-through. The bug gets discussed, everyone agrees, and then the thread disappears.

With Sharkly's Slack integration, the path from conversation to code is much shorter:

  1. Mention the Task assistant in the thread, or use a message shortcut
  2. Keep the thread bound to the Task so updates flow both ways
  3. Assign a coding agent like you'd assign a teammate
  4. Link the PR with the Task ID and review it as usual

The context from Slack travels with the work, the agent gets a clear task, and the people who raised the issue see it resolved in the same thread.

If you want to try it, you can get started at sharkly.ai.

items.title: I landed 4 job offers out of grad school and picked Meta. These 2 tactics helped me land my ideal offer.
items.summary: Adwait Sathe shared how he landed four job offers after grad school. Adwait Sathe Adwait Sathe, a data privacy engineer at Meta, went into his job hunt five years ago with a plan. He was strategic about who he cold-messaged on LinkedIn, and how he tailored his CV to each application. He said that if he were applying for the same roles today, he would be sure to stack up on side projects. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Adwait Sathe, a 32-year-old senior data privacy engineer at Meta Superintelligence Labs. It has been edited for length and clarity. I've been working at Meta for the last five years, first at Messenger, and for the last three years as a data privacy engineer at Meta Superintelligence Labs . I moved to the US from India in 2019 to pursue a master's degree in information systems at Northeastern University in Boston, graduating in 2021. I knew the job application process out of college would be competitive, so I started my job search about a year and a half before I graduated. I was very clear from the start: I want to work in data engineering privacy. I took classes in that field and built a relevant portfolio through internships and side projects . In my second semester, I started looking at job postings I would apply for a year later to understand what the industry was looking for. I had four offers in hand when I graduated — from McKinsey, Walmart, Amazon, and Meta. Here's the strategy I used to approach my job search. Cold messaging people who weren't too senior I had a tactic for cold messaging people on LinkedIn. I connected with a lot of people on LinkedIn who were working on things similar to what I wanted to work on. The people I reached out to were active on LinkedIn and working in Big Tech in data engineering roles, not managerial roles. Engineers and senior engineers, not vice presidents or directors. I was looking for mentorship. I approached them to understand the industry's requirements, so that when I applied, my application would stand out among the masses. My cold message was very simple: "Hey, I am Adwait, I'm studying this, and I want to pursue my career in this. I have this tech stack and résumé; what should I improve?" One connection gave me excellent advice — that my résumé made it look like I wasn't experienced. I had three years of work experience in India after getting my bachelor's degree. Still, when I first put together my résumé, it looked like a new grad résumé because I front-loaded my education over my work experience. I started getting more interviews when I fixed that issue. When I started cold messaging with this strategy, I aimed for volume, sending messages to a lot of people. Many didn't reply. But once I had gotten three or four good mentors, I eased up on messaging, knowing that these people were really solid and would help me out. I've tried to pass it on. Now, I reply to almost all LinkedIn messages I receive that ask for career advice. Splitting job apps by volume and strategy My second job search strategy was to split my application process into two buckets. The first bucket: companies I really wanted to work for. I had a list of companies I wanted to work for, and I used to go to their career websites a couple of times a week to check for new positions and apply early. I would be looking out for new grad positions, which are typically released way before graduation season. The second bucket was wider. This was all about volume, applying to as many roles as possible. I had a generic résumé for all the volume-based applications. But for the ones I really wanted, I tailored each application. After I got my first offer, a data engineering role at Walmart, I stopped applying in volume. The strategy after that was to apply for roles I really wanted, which could match or exceed what I'd already gotten. How I would apply differently today with AI If I were applying for the same roles today, I would make sure to have a lot of different projects in my portfolio, because building has become so important. A working product, which is live and has real users, is way better than bringing a prototype into the interview and saying, "I built this prototype, it worked when I built it, but it's not working now." The second thing is AI fluency. This doesn't just mean understanding different tools, but also how AI works in the background and a judgment of when to use which tools. But the fundamentals don't change. Being good at coding and knowing how to structure the code is still important. AI can handle implementation, but designing systems and architecture is still very important and human. Read the original article on Business Insider

But once I had gotten three or four good mentors, I eased up on messaging, knowing that these people were really solid and would help me out.

I've tried to pass it on. Now, I reply to almost all LinkedIn messages I receive that ask for career advice.

Splitting job apps by volume and strategy

My second job search strategy was to split my application process into two buckets.

The first bucket: companies I really wanted to work for.

I had a list of companies I wanted to work for, and I used to go to their career websites a couple of times a week to check for new positions and apply early. I would be looking out for new grad positions, which are typically released way before graduation season.

The second bucket was wider. This was all about volume, applying to as many roles as possible.

I had a generic résumé for all the volume-based applications. But for the ones I really wanted, I tailored each application.

After I got my first offer, a data engineering role at Walmart, I stopped applying in volume. The strategy after that was to apply for roles I really wanted, which could match or exceed what I'd already gotten.

How I would apply differently today with AI

If I were applying for the same roles today, I would make sure to have a lot of different projects in my portfolio, because building has become so important.

A working product, which is live and has real users, is way better than bringing a prototype into the interview and saying, "I built this prototype, it worked when I built it, but it's not working now."

The second thing is AI fluency. This doesn't just mean understanding different tools, but also how AI works in the background and a judgment of when to use which tools.

But the fundamentals don't change. Being good at coding and knowing how to structure the code is still important. AI can handle implementation, but designing systems and architecture is still very important and human.

items.title: Can You Trust Your ‘Instinct’ and Not ‘Muse’ Over the Risks?
items.summary: A string of incidents—from the HuggingFace breach to the Australian government fiasco—has made AI agent safety risks impossible to dismiss. More unsettling, this may be only the opening act. OpenAI is reportedly spending half a million dollars a day investigating past AI incidents, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development. Yet as companies figure out how to keep these AI agents and their behaviours in check, they're racing to put them in the hands of millions. AI agents today—the ones that can use your web browser and autonomously perform tasks—are getting more intuitive. They no longer need the complex assembly only developers could do; they’re now baked into chatbots. Share your login credentials, and the AI agent will swim through an application and get what you need. Instinct, a personal AI agent designed to plan trips, buy groceries, book tickets, and cancel subscriptions, raised $1 billion in September at a $10 billion valuation, just a month after an earlier round valued it at $2.5 billion. Meanwhile, Meta’s Muse AI agent has found 10 million users within six weeks of launch. OpenAI has launched Dots, its always-on agents designed to work across apps, while Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet. Newer personal AI agent startups are jostling to attract what seems to be easy AI money. Tab emerged at a $300 million valuation, and Eden Labs raised $1.5 million to build an agent that can navigate apps and the web to complete everyday tasks. Consumers are at a crossroads between convenience and caution. These AI agents offer an irresistible appeal: automating tasks people hate and aren’t skilled at. But the risks of handing these agents access to personal accounts, sensitive data, and the authority to act on their behalf are just as difficult to ignore. Are Consumer AI Agents Safe? How can users be sure an AI agent will not misuse access to their accounts? For instance, an agent ordering food may be able to interact with a logged-in account and access payment options. If it makes a mistake or is manipulated into taking an unintended action, the consequences could extend beyond a wrong recommendation to an unauthorised purchase. A virtual machine, where the agent operates in an isolated cloud environment, can help contain the damage by blocking access to local, personal information stored on the device. But it doesn’t prevent the agent from misusing permissions and capabilities it has already been granted. “The attacker doesn’t need to escape. Everything they want is already reachable [on the VM],” Vrajesh Bhavsar, Co-founder and CEO of Operant AI, a cybersecurity platform for AI agents, tells AIM. If an agent can read emails, access files, or use logged-in browser sessions, an attacker may exploit those capabilities without breaking out of the virtual machine. One way is through prompt injection, where malicious instructions hidden in an email or webpage trick the agent into disclosing sensitive information or taking actions the user never authorised. Meta says it has trained its Muse agent to recognise and resist prompt injection. It also labels information arriving from external sources as untrusted and runs multiple independent classifiers to detect malicious instructions in content entering the agent's context. These checks extend to text, images, downloaded files, and webpages. The company has also built safeguards outside the AI model. A separate security component, called Sentinel, mediates the agent's internet access and decides whether an action can proceed. However, Meta acknowledges that Muse is not immune to attacks. While safeguards can reduce the likelihood of manipulation, prompt injection remains an open problem. The company has opened a public bug bounty programme offering up to $300,000 for valid security reports, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt-injection attacks affecting a single user. “Large language models read instructions and data in the same stream, so they can’t reliably tell a user’s request from text planted in a web page,” notes Devendra Rath, VP of Engineering at cybersecurity company Arctic Wolf. “Developers should design as if an injection will eventually succeed and limit the damage.” Rath explains that this means restricting agents to the minimum permissions each task requires and separating the component that reads untrusted content from the one authorised to take action. Developers should also block pathways that could let agents leak sensitive information, such as malicious instructions that make an agent embed private data in an image URL. And what about passwords? Muse requires user approval for actions that move data outside its virtual machine, while its email connector filters out one-time passcodes, password-reset links, and login links that could be exploited to take over other accounts. Meta says Muse keeps users’ actual passwords in a separate, protected store that the AI cannot directly access. Across these agents, credentials are also short-lived and not stored beyond what is necessary for a task, and highly sensitive actions such as changing passwords aren't possible without users taking over. Can Data Ever Be Deleted? The other concern, however, is also what happens to personal user data when an agent is disconnected—or deleted. Even after deletion, Rath says, “Several kinds of data can remain. These include the VM disk, saved credentials and tokens, activity logs, backups, and derived memories such as summaries and embeddings.” Similarly, Bhavsar advises users to revoke the agent’s authentication grants in whichever service it is connected to, rather than relying on the agent’s disconnect button. “Rotate any credentials the agent could see. Then ask the vendor for its retention and deletion policy in writing, including whether derived memories and embeddings are deleted along with the raw data.” Agents today let users disconnect tools and services and delete their chats. But that isn’t everything. “Agent data lives in more places than people realise: conversation logs, vector stores and long-term memory, cached files, authorisation tokens, debugging logs, and others”, says Bhavsar. Meta says its ‘Forget’ function searches the agent's memories and supporting files to remove information about a topic “to the best of its ability.” Websites are Blocking Agents That said, these agents have already caused concern. Last month, The Information reported that a security researcher discovered a vulnerability in Meta’s Muse that could have let an attacker access a user’s dedicated virtual machine, which stores sensitive information such as emails and files. According to an internal incident report the publication reviewed, Meta initially classified the flaw as a SEV-2 incident, its third-highest severity level. The vulnerability was reported through Meta’s bug bounty programme. While there was no public evidence that the flaw was exploited to steal user data, Meta subsequently said it was adding a clearer safety warning within Muse . Instinct has also faced questions about unauthorised actions and data retention. In August, early users reported that the agent had sent an email without approval and continued summarising previously indexed emails hours after a Gmail connection was disconnected. Instinct explained that it stored the emails in plain text for search, highlighting the distinction between revoking access to an account and deleting data already copied from it. Last month, X user Pritak alleged that Instinct had surfaced someone else’s financial information in a conversation and referred to a photograph the user said they had never uploaded. The incident raised concerns about whether the agent could expose data across users. Instinct just admitted it leaked someone else's data to me It described a financial document with details that weren’t mine, then claimed someone else’s photo had crossed into my chat. But I never sent a photo @noahrshinn, was this a data leak or a hallucination? https://t.co/nev6t7w85k — Pritak (@prit4k) September 21, 2026 Instinct attributed the incident to a hallucination in which the model fabricated a proper noun, compounded by its internal reasoning trace. The company said it had not shared any user data and had not violated any isolation boundary. It also said it developed a hallucination-detection system that scans and verifies tokens and can interrupt the model before it generates further reasoning or executes a tool call. Despite efforts and guardrails to keep these agents safe, several websites now block AI agents. Amazon has blocked Meta’s Muse from browsing its retail catalogue and making purchases, while users have reported similar problems with Instinct and OpenAI’s Dots. Yelp permits AI agents to access its content only through its paid data-licensing programme, and Delta Air Lines prevents agents from booking tickets on users’ behalf. But for how long? Salesforce has predicted that 20% of holiday e-commerce traffic this year will come from a mix of real shoppers’ agents and price-scraping bots. “Personal agents shop on real customers’ behalf, but to legacy defences, an authorised agent looks just like a malicious bot, which is why Amazon has blocked Muse, citing security concerns,” Bhavsar says. However, he believes blocking all agents aggressively can “turn away real customers and their agents during the busiest sales season of the year.” “The fix is to judge each action, not just the visitor at the door. Treat every agent as an accountable identity that can be tracked and stopped at runtime, and check each transaction against what the customer actually asked for before it goes through,” he says.

Consumers are at a crossroads between convenience and caution. These AI agents offer an irresistible appeal: automating tasks people hate and aren’t skilled at. But the risks of handing these agents access to personal accounts, sensitive data, and the authority to act on their behalf are just as difficult to ignore.

Are Consumer AI Agents Safe?

How can users be sure an AI agent will not misuse access to their accounts? 

For instance, an agent ordering food may be able to interact with a logged-in account and access payment options. If it makes a mistake or is manipulated into taking an unintended action, the consequences could extend beyond a wrong recommendation to an unauthorised purchase.

A virtual machine, where the agent operates in an isolated cloud environment, can help contain the damage by blocking access to local, personal information stored on the device. But it doesn’t prevent the agent from misusing permissions and capabilities it has already been granted.

“The attacker doesn’t need to escape. Everything they want is already reachable [on the VM],” Vrajesh Bhavsar, Co-founder and CEO of Operant AI, a cybersecurity platform for AI agents, tells AIM.

If an agent can read emails, access files, or use logged-in browser sessions, an attacker may exploit those capabilities without breaking out of the virtual machine. One way is through prompt injection, where malicious instructions hidden in an email or webpage trick the agent into disclosing sensitive information or taking actions the user never authorised.

Meta says it has trained its Muse agent to recognise and resist prompt injection. It also labels information arriving from external sources as untrusted and runs multiple independent classifiers to detect malicious instructions in content entering the agent's context. 

These checks extend to text, images, downloaded files, and webpages. 

The company has also built safeguards outside the AI model. A separate security component, called Sentinel, mediates the agent's internet access and decides whether an action can proceed. 

However, Meta acknowledges that Muse is not immune to attacks. While safeguards can reduce the likelihood of manipulation, prompt injection remains an open problem. 

The company has opened a public bug bounty programme offering up to $300,000 for valid security reports, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt-injection attacks affecting a single user.

“Large language models read instructions and data in the same stream, so they can’t reliably tell a user’s request from text planted in a web page,” notes Devendra Rath, VP of Engineering at cybersecurity company Arctic Wolf. “Developers should design as if an injection will eventually succeed and limit the damage.”

Rath explains that this means restricting agents to the minimum permissions each task requires and separating the component that reads untrusted content from the one authorised to take action. Developers should also block pathways that could let agents leak sensitive information, such as malicious instructions that make an agent embed private data in an image URL. 

And what about passwords? 

Muse requires user approval for actions that move data outside its virtual machine, while its email connector filters out one-time passcodes, password-reset links, and login links that could be exploited to take over other accounts. Meta says Muse keeps users’ actual passwords in a separate, protected store that the AI cannot directly access. 

Across these agents, credentials are also short-lived and not stored beyond what is necessary for a task, and highly sensitive actions such as changing passwords aren't possible without users taking over. 

Can Data Ever Be Deleted?

The other concern, however, is also what happens to personal user data when an agent is disconnected—or deleted. 

Even after deletion, Rath says, “Several kinds of data can remain. These include the VM disk, saved credentials and tokens, activity logs, backups, and derived memories such as summaries and embeddings.”

Similarly, Bhavsar advises users to revoke the agent’s authentication grants in whichever service it is connected to, rather than relying on the agent’s disconnect button. “Rotate any credentials the agent could see. Then ask the vendor for its retention and deletion policy in writing, including whether derived memories and embeddings are deleted along with the raw data.” 

Agents today let users disconnect tools and services and delete their chats. But that isn’t everything. “Agent data lives in more places than people realise: conversation logs, vector stores and long-term memory, cached files, authorisation tokens, debugging logs, and others”, says Bhavsar. 

Meta says its ‘Forget’ function searches the agent's memories and supporting files to remove information about a topic “to the best of its ability.”

Websites are Blocking Agents

That said, these agents have already caused concern. 

Last month, The Information reported that a security researcher discovered a vulnerability in Meta’s Muse that could have let an attacker access a user’s dedicated virtual machine, which stores sensitive information such as emails and files. 

According to an internal incident report the publication reviewed, Meta initially classified the flaw as a SEV-2 incident, its third-highest severity level. The vulnerability was reported through Meta’s bug bounty programme. 

While there was no public evidence that the flaw was exploited to steal user data, Meta subsequently said it was adding a clearer safety warning within Muse.

Instinct has also faced questions about unauthorised actions and data retention. 

In August, early users reported that the agent had sent an email without approval and continued summarising previously indexed emails hours after a Gmail connection was disconnected. Instinct explained that it stored the emails in plain text for search, highlighting the distinction between revoking access to an account and deleting data already copied from it.

Last month, X user Pritak alleged that Instinct had surfaced someone else’s financial information in a conversation and referred to a photograph the user said they had never uploaded. The incident raised concerns about whether the agent could expose data across users.

Instinct just admitted it leaked someone else's data to me It described a financial document with details that weren’t mine, then claimed someone else’s photo had crossed into my chat. But I never sent a photo @noahrshinn, was this a data leak or a hallucination? https://t.co/nev6t7w85k
— Pritak (@prit4k) September 21, 2026


Instinct attributed the incident to a hallucination in which the model fabricated a proper noun, compounded by its internal reasoning trace. 

The company said it had not shared any user data and had not violated any isolation boundary. It also said it developed a hallucination-detection system that scans and verifies tokens and can interrupt the model before it generates further reasoning or executes a tool call.

Despite efforts and guardrails to keep these agents safe, several websites now block AI agents. 

Amazon has blocked Meta’s Muse from browsing its retail catalogue and making purchases, while users have reported similar problems with Instinct and OpenAI’s Dots. Yelp permits AI agents to access its content only through its paid data-licensing programme, and Delta Air Lines prevents agents from booking tickets on users’ behalf.

Salesforce has predicted that 20% of holiday e-commerce traffic this year will come from a mix of real shoppers’ agents and price-scraping bots.

However, he believes blocking all agents aggressively can “turn away real customers and their agents during the busiest sales season of the year.” 

“The fix is to judge each action, not just the visitor at the door. Treat every agent as an accountable identity that can be tracked and stopped at runtime, and check each transaction against what the customer actually asked for before it goes through,” he says.

items.title: Anthropic Seeks Up to $64.4 Bn at $1.4 Tn Valuation With IPO
items.summary: Anthropic has launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering (IPO), offering 825 million shares of Class A common stock at an indicative price range of $70–78 per share. The offering could raise up to $64.4 billion, valuing the Claude maker at approximately $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. The roadshow follows a series of regulatory filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Anthropic initially filed its Form S-1 registration statement on October 26, followed by a recent amendment. Of the 825 million shares on offer, Anthropic is selling 801.35 million, while existing shareholders are selling the remaining 23.65 million. The company will not receive proceeds from the shares sold by existing investors. It has also proposed a 30-day underwriters' option to purchase an additional 123.75 million shares. Separately, Anthropic is expected to raise another $26 billion through a private placement involving institutional investors. Google, NVIDIA, and AMD are among the cornerstone investors, and combined with the IPO, the transactions could generate up to $90.4 billion. Anthropic's prospectus shows that its revenue reached $33.2 billion in the nine months ended September 30, compared with $2.5 billion during the corresponding period last year, representing over 13x growth. For the third quarter , revenue stood at approximately $17 billion, up from $1.4 billion in the same quarter last year. However, the company reported an operating loss of $567 million for the quarter, reversing the $974 million operating profit recorded in Q2. It also reported more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual recurring revenue. Anthropic has approximately $900 billion in aggregate committed spending on compute infrastructure and related agreements. Around $70.7 billion of these commitments are due within the next 12 months.

items.title: IBM Ends H-1B, Green Card Sponsorship for Most Roles in Consulting Division
items.summary: IBM is ending US H-1B visa and green card sponsorship for a majority of roles in its consulting division, which employs more than 150,000 people worldwide, according to Bloomberg . The decision will affect foreign workers seeking employer-sponsored immigration support to work in the US, with impacted employees reportedly being given the option to transfer to IBM positions outside the country or leave the company by the end of 2026. Reuters subsequently reported that IBM confirmed the decision, citing changes in the availability of skilled workers and client requirements. A company spokesperson said IBM had historically used high-skilled visa programmes to address talent shortages, but its participation had been declining for several years. “That participation has been declining for a number of years,” the spokesperson told Reuters , adding that IBM had decided to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for most such roles in IBM Consulting. US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) data shows that IBM received 2,045 H-1B petition approvals in FY25, down 29.7% from 2,906 in FY24. The decline was concentrated in applications for new employment, which fell 62.8% from 1,348 to 501 during the same period. Of the 2,045 approvals in FY25, 501 were for initial employment, while 1,544 were for continuing employment, which includes visa extensions, amendments, and changes of employer. Initial-employment approvals accounted for just 24.5% of IBM's total approvals, compared with 46.4% in FY2024. The trend continued into FY2026. IBM received 1,611 approvals between October 2025 and June 2026, comprising 708 initial-employment and 903 continuing-employment approvals. These are partial-year figures and should not be directly compared with full-year totals. Bloomberg cited an internal company document shared with managers in the consulting division. According to the document, affected employees can continue working for IBM outside the US or leave the company by the end of the year. IBM's decision comes amid the US President Donald Trump administration's tightening of employment-based immigration programmes. In September 2025, the White House announced a one-time $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions for workers hired from outside the US. The company is also joining a growing list of technology and IT services companies facing restrictions on employment-based immigration. Last month, the US Department of Labor suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant , Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme. The suspension prevents these companies from filing new or processing pending PERM applications, a key step in the employer-sponsored green card process.

items.title: PuppyGraph Raises $10 Mn to Help AI Agents Query Enterprise Tables
items.summary: PuppyGraph, a graph query engine startup for enterprise artificial intelligence (AI), has raised $10 million in a Series A round led by Particle Future, with participation from defy.vc. “The insights of enterprise data will soon be generated by agents,” Weimo Liu, Co-founder and CEO of PuppyGraph, said in a statement. He added that agents would need to navigate thousands of tables, follow relationships, and retrieve evidence across departments and systems. The funding takes the US-based company’s total capital raised to $15 million and will support engineering and enterprise go-to-market expansion, the company said. The announcement follows the general availability of PuppyGraph 1.0, which allows AI agents to query data across up to 3,000 enterprise tables as a unified graph without transferring the underlying data into a separate graph database, the company said. According to PuppyGraph, AI agent projects that initially cover 30–50 tables can become difficult to scale when production workloads require connections across thousands of tables and multiple systems. It also enforces configured row-level permissions during graph traversals and offers role-based access controls and single sign-on. Its annual recurring revenue grew sevenfold over the past year, although it did not disclose the revenue figure. “For a user-facing application, query latency and data freshness are non-negotiable. PuppyGraph allows us to execute multi-hop graph traversals directly on our existing data platform without moving or duplicating a single row,” said Ran Xia, Engineering Director at Palo Alto Networks. The company said that developers can access PuppyGraph through a free Docker deployment, without submitting a payment method or registration form.

items.title: Cognizant Commits 25,000 Professionals to Deploy Claude in Enterprises
items.summary: Cognizant has committed more than 25,000 professionals to deploying Anthropic's Claude for enterprise clients. The IT services company has also introduced a managed services model under which it will operate Claude-powered systems in production on behalf of clients. The model combines dedicated personnel, licensed access to Claude, and Cognizant's proprietary software. "Clients want a partner who will take responsibility for delivery once AI is running inside their business," Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant, said in a statement. "We are putting more than 25,000 of our people on Claude and taking on the job of running it for clients through managed services." The announcement builds on Cognizant's expanded partnership with Anthropic in July, when it outlined plans to integrate Claude into its engineering platforms. Cognizant said more than 44,000 associates across its business units and corporate functions had been trained or certified on Claude. It also reported more than 26,000 Claude certifications. The group will focus on applying AI to business processes, modernising existing systems, deploying and managing AI agents, and using AI in software development. Cognizant will also use Claude-powered agents to analyse and refactor legacy code, including mainframe systems. Other Indian IT services companies are also building teams around frontier AI models. HCLTech signed a partnership with Anthropic in October, establishing a dedicated business unit and a Centre of Excellence for Claude-based enterprise solutions. "Every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organisation, but the people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find," said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer at Anthropic. "Cognizant is working to address that gap, committing more than 25,000 people to help their customers put Claude to work across their businesses." Under the managed services model, Cognizant will operate Claude-powered systems in production for clients. The company said the offering would provide more predictable AI spending, with security and governance controls tailored to each client's requirements. It did not disclose the commercial terms.

items.title: From Relevant Posts to Attributable Spans: Explicit Symptom Evidence for Depression Questionnaire Inference
items.summary: Longitudinal social-media histories offer an opportunity to assess depression, potentially supporting the inference of standardized depression questionnaire responses. However, this task requires evidence that is semantically relevant to a symptom and attributable to the user, while being sufficiently specific to support an individual questionnaire item. Existing approaches rely on semantic similarity to retrieve posts, which can introduce misleading or non-attributable evidence, particularly in multi-symptom posts and discussions of others' experiences. We propose SREE (Symptom Retrieval and Evidence-Grounded InfErence), an evidence-grounded pipeline that extracts first-person and symptom-specific text spans, selects a representative subset using a Facility Location-inspired objective, and performs Evidence-Gated Inference over the selected evidence. We evaluate evidence retrieval on BDI-Sen and evidence-conditioned questionnaire inference on eRisk 2019-2021. Compared with state-of-the-art retrieval approaches, SREE achieves relative improvements of 70% in post-level precision and 59% in F1, while retaining at least 30% fewer posts. On multi-symptom sentences, it also outperforms dense retrieval in precision and F1 even with twice the retrieval budget. Across all three eRisk collections, SREE achieves the highest exact item-level agreement while remaining competitive on ordinal and aggregate metrics. These results highlight the importance of localizing attributable evidence and controlling its composition before inferring depression questionnaire responses.

items.title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
items.summary: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

items.title: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting
items.summary: Time series from real-world systems are often accompanied by text, such as a report on an event that affects them. Two common tasks on these series are understanding, e.g., answering questions about a series, and forecasting its future values. Both tasks require reasoning over the series and the text together. Moreover, understanding outputs text while forecasting outputs a time series, so serving both requires a model that reads and generates both modalities. Large language models (LLMs) read time series as digit tokens and handle long series poorly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast well from large-scale pretraining but typically neither read nor generate text. Time series language models add a time series modality to the LLM but forecast on the LLM side, leaving the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability unused. We present TimeOmni-o1, which couples a pretrained TSFM and an LLM bidirectionally. In one direction, the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM, which reasons over it together with the text. In the other, the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM, which produces the forecast conditioned on it. One model architecture thus reads and generates both series and text, reasons in text, and draws on the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability. To train it, we build MMTR, a multimodal time series reasoning dataset with annotated reasoning traces, covering both tasks across 12 domains with 500k+ samples. On MMTR, TimeOmni-o1 outperforms existing models on both understanding and forecasting across most domains, as well as the LLM and the TSFM inside it when used individually. The gains carry over to three open benchmarks, where it outperforms the dedicated time series models.

items.title: SELD: Detecting Silent Evidence Loss in Context Compression beyond the Answer
items.summary: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.

items.title: Actionable Feedback: Improving Model Capabilities from User Edit Data on Clinical Documentation
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in clinical documentation workflows, where clinicians review and edit their outputs before use. In principle, these clinician edits represent a scalable source of supervision for model training. In practice, not all edits represent actionable feedback: for instance, on data drawn from real-world deployment of an AI clinical documentation product, our review suggests that over 45% of edited outputs contain user-added information that is not directly supported by the inputs to the model. Naively fine-tuning on such edits risks teaching the model to hallucinate. In this paper, we develop a method to address this challenge. Given that real clinician edits on deployed documentation tools are not publicly available, we first develop a taxonomy of clinician-editing behaviors, informed by data from a deployed AI clinical documentation product. Then, we develop a method for generating semi-synthetic clinician-edit data, informed by our taxonomy, on a discharge-summary generation task based on MIMIC-III, a public dataset. Finally, we introduce simple filtering methods for identifying actionable edits, with accuracy evaluated by expert review. We show empirically, on our semi-synthetic dataset, that naive fine-tuning on raw edited output increases ungrounded content, while our approach of progressively filtering toward grounded edits enables improvement on clinician-alignment metrics while retaining faithfulness to the input context.

items.title: Brasilidade: Measuring Brazilian Identity for Large Language Models
items.summary: This work presents a new benchmark that aims to address the limitations of current methods for evaluating LLMs in Brazilian Portuguese. We introduced Brasilidade, an assessment methodology comprised of standardized tasks distributed across four different domains, and we are making available the tasks from its first domain, which address nuances of the language, grammar, and variations of Brazilian Portuguese. The results show that model size, by itself, does not determine performance; several medium-sized models outperformed larger models in the protocols evaluated. Specific models for Portuguese, in general, did not perform above average, despite their targeted training. Different task levels revealed significant nuances: while some tasks proved easy for most models, others posed extreme challenges, and some yielded mixed results, with wide variations in performance. This clearly illustrates the need for benchmarks that address the limitations of the models in Brazilian Portuguese, allowing future training cycles to seek to overcome them. Project repository https://github.com/soberania-oficial/brasilidade

items.title: IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap in Offline Web Behavior Prediction
items.summary: Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. We show that this protocol can create a candidate-support confound: when the target is outside training support while all distractors are sampled from that support, support membership identifies the gold action without modeling behavior. We formalize this effect with support-identifiability rate (SIR), construct support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer that combines support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM/LM proposals. On filtered OPeRA (4,282/469/992 train/dev/test steps), the original protocol has SIR 1.0000 on target-OOV rows and a support-only rule reaches 1.0000 OOV Exact@1. Support balancing reduces SIR to 0.0000; the strongest conditional reranker obtains 0.7214 overall Exact@1, 0.7988 on IV rows, and 0.5668 on OOV rows. The target-free dual-path system reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.5212, compared with oracle conditional Exact@1 0.7450. On Mind2Web, the same audit yields SIR 0.2380 and an oracle-to-proposal gap of 0.2125. A 200-row semantic audit labels 0.7150 of exact-key OOV targets as semantically novel, 0.2450 as locator/string variation, and 0.0400 as ambiguous (Cohen's $\kappa=0.8173$). These measurements show why support composition must be controlled alongside candidate accuracy when offline results are used to reason about deployment.

items.title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing
items.summary: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.

items.title: khammoon: From a Linguistic Guideline to a Thai Morpheme Segmenter
items.summary: Thai is written without spaces between words, making segmentation a foundational step in most Thai NLP pipelines. Existing tools primarily reproduce the word-level conventions of corpora such as BEST; however, because the notion of a "word" in Thai lacks a unified linguistic consensus, these conventions struggle with productive compounding, leading to arbitrary boundaries and ambiguity in downstream representations. Instead, we propose operating at the morphological level, focusing on khammoon, the smallest atomic unit that carries meaning. Segmenting at the morphemic level provides an explicit, consistent morphological representation that eliminates compounding ambiguity. Crucially, this representation benefits downstream learning: models trained on morphemes perform on par with or exceed word-level baselines across part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment classification, demonstrating that linguistic consistency improves representation quality without downstream performance penalty. To operationalize this representation, we translate linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement ($\kappa \approx 0.99$), scale annotation with an LLM, and correct systematic errors with human labels. Finally, we train khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, achieving a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text. The guideline, datasets, model, and library are all publicly released.

items.title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
items.summary: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.

items.title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
items.summary: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.

items.title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.

items.title: HiCAP: Hierarchical Cultural Adaptation via Personality for Dialogue Generation
items.summary: Cultural adaptation in dialogue systems refers to the ability to generate responses that conform to linguistic norms and social expectations across different cultures. However, existing dialogue generation approaches pay limited attention to the role of personality in shaping cultural expression and communication style. We therefore propose HiCAP, a novel framework that integrates personality traits into culturally adaptive dialogue generation. HiCAP employs a personality-conditioned control mechanism that hierarchically modulates response style by first aligning it with the cultural tone and then refining linguistic expression and content according to individual personality attributes. To embed these factors, the model combines supervised fine-tuning and instruction-based tuning, supported by dynamic instruction templates and multi-agent demonstrations to capture diverse combinations of culture and personality. Experiments on CulturalPersonas and CPED show that HiCAP achieves the strongest overall performance across various dialogue generation metrics, demonstrating effective cultural adaptability and personality modelling.

items.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
items.summary: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

items.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
items.summary: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

items.title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
items.summary: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

items.title: Understanding Students' Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis
items.summary: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty.

items.title: Mapping Instructors' Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
items.summary: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of large language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students' academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with Generative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers' motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration.

items.title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
