items.title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
items.summary: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

items.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
items.summary: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

items.title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
items.summary: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

items.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
items.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

items.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
items.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

items.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
items.summary: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

items.title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

items.title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
items.summary: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.

items.title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
items.summary: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. “This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote. They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual. The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said. The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla. Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode. “ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic. “Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said. This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted. Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory. Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said. A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy. Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said. His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process. But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described. “A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.” ‘A level above’ And, said David Shipley , CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.” Running on premises Exchange has been increasingly risky for years, he noted. For government, AI firms, finance, and other high-value targets, the risk of hosting on prem instead of using cloud-based versions continues to grow. However, it’s worth noting that just having Microsoft host Exchange doesn’t mean you’re safe from nation-states, Shipley said. “It just raises the bar.” Another key challenge with Exchange servers is Microsoft’s own advice not to have anti-virus scanners looking in certain places like ExchangeTransport.exe, because doing so could create instability. “They basically told criminals where to hide and why it’s good to hide there,” he noted. “Not that they can do much about it, but it points to a huge Catch-22.” Another Catch-22: With the publication of this report and new ideas that will undoubtedly come from it, “we’ll likely see criminal groups consider the value of this kind of technique in the future,” Shipley noted.

There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders.

A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage.

The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks.

While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies, enterprises should still be concerned.

“Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.”

Sophisticated tradecraft

ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk.

The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part.

Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. 

“This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote.

They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual.

The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said.

The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla.

“ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic.

“Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said.

This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted.

Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself into Exchange’s mail process and wraps the agents already running in memory.

Mail keeps flowing, but nothing new appears. “It is the postal carrier who steams open the envelope, copies the letter, and reseals it before delivery,” Dickson said.

A component dubbed CerealBox selects messages with .doc, .docx, and .pdf attachments from chosen senders, recipients, and subjects. In Romania, ESET discovered that it collected mail involving The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)  and EU addresses. This should concern enterprises, Dickson said; swap in your preferred targets: outside counsel, your acquisition target, or your regulator, to retrieve a contract, a deal memo, or a legal strategy.

Further, the commands ESET documented include pulling entire mailboxes, extracting credentials stored on the server, and querying Active Directory for users, groups, and computers. An Exchange server sits deep inside the identity fabric. It is an Achilles’ heel because it is internet-facing, highly privileged, and complex. “Own it, and you hold the keys to the kingdom if you will,” Dickson said.

His advice: Migrate or retire on premises Exchange where possible. Treat whatever remains as a tier-zero asset, “guarded like a domain controller.” Limit internet exposure of Outlook Web Access and ActiveSync to what the business truly needs. Hunt with the indicators described by ESET. Watch for unexpected code loading into Exchange’s transport process.

But while the researchers’ work is excellent because it maps what Turla did once inside an organization in “remarkable detail,” it does not say how Turla got onto those servers, Dickson pointed out. No vulnerability is named, and no stolen credential or phishing email is described.

“A burglar who leaves no fingerprints is impressive,” said Dickson. “A burglar whose way in remains unknown is a problem for every house on the street.”

And, said David Shipley, CEO of Beauceron Security, we’ve seen the gap between nation state hackers and criminals collapse over the past few years in terms of sophistication, in particular thanks to AI, but “then you see something like this, which is still a level above.”

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.summary: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task on the web and showed me that its Appshot (a new feature enabling you to save an app experience to ChatGPT) was still there. For a task that started locally, he described asking Codex to push a branch and start a new cloud thread. Codex Cloud is now as “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user. The first is as a safety net — your dot can flag things you may have missed. The second is as “a delegation sink” ; Guo said he uses it “a ton in Slack” for this reason. And the third is as a ubiquitous presence . “I think the third way that dots are a little bit different is we're aiming to make them truly everywhere that you work ,” Guo said. For his part, Kundel told me that he starts off a lot of his tasks from his dot, rather than by prompting Codex itself. “And that's because it often already has a lot of the context and understands how to manage things, and it can push these PRs forward for me.” Conclusion Kundel ended the workshop with a list of tips to use on Codex, including “turn it down” (meaning the effort level) and to “ask your agents for help.” But ultimately, he said, the key is to not get too attached to your current way of working in Codex — “things are constantly changing.”

items.title: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms
items.summary: Fish Audio has released Live 3 , a full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents. The Fish Audio Live 3 full-duplex voice model keeps listening while it speaks. That lets a caller pause, say “mm-hmm,” or change their mind without breaking the call. For developers, the pitch is simple. Turn-taking moves out of hand-tuned pipeline rules and into the speech model. TL;DR Product: A full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents Runs on: Hosted Fish Agent Platform and Fish Audio API; on-premises for enterprises. Performance: Fish Audio shows behavior demos, but publishes no benchmark scores. Best: Can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms for short reactions like “mm-hmm.” What is Fish Audio Live 3? Live 3 is a full-duplex voice model from Fish Audio that listens and speaks at the same time. The core argument is that speed and timing are different problems. An agent can reply fast and still speak at the wrong moment. A pause after “What time do you open?” usually ends a turn. A pause in the middle of a phone number does not. How does Live 3 handle turn-taking? Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and turn-taking across separate pipeline stages. Fish Audio team states that Live 3 moves conversational timing into the speech model. It was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop. They framed the old approach as piling on “more rules and more thresholds.” Fish Audio instead wants the model to learn timing from data. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent’s instructions and tools. The Fish Audio team walks through 3 behaviors: Acknowledging without taking over. A caller reads “415… 555… 0132.” Live 3 may say “okay, 415” between chunks, then wait. Telling a backchannel from an interruption. A caller saying “yeah” lets the agent continue. “Wait, actually, I just need Thursday” makes it stop. Waiting through corrections. For “two pizzas… no, three,” Live 3 waits instead of logging the wrong order. How fast is Live 3? Fish Audio states Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms . That figure covers short reactions such as “mm-hmm,” “okay” and quick confirmations. The full answer is prepared in parallel. This is a floor for small reactions, not time-to-first-audio for a complete reply. Fish Audio has not published a latency distribution. Third-party tracker OrcaRouter also reports no Artificial Analysis score for Live 3 as of November 11. & How do developers deploy Live 3? Live 3 is available on the Fish Agent Platform , through the Fish Audio API, and on-premises for enterprises. The Agents platform is in public beta. Agents expose a REST surface under /v1/agent/* . Browser sessions run through @fishaudio/agent-client or @fishaudio/agent-react . Agents can answer phone numbers, connect over WebRTC, or sit in a website widget. The Live 3 page lists 2,000,000+ library voices, including cloned voices. A pending docs pull request shows Live 3 enabled with voice.engine: "live3" . With it on, speech recognition is fixed to fish_audio:transcribe-stream-1 . Fish Audio’s current docs say that model also classifies overlaps as interruptions or acknowledgements. How much does Live 3 cost? The Live 3 page lists $0.035 per minute , down 50% from $0.07 , until December 31, 2026. It says the plan includes Live 3. The pricing docs say the $0.07 list rate covers STT, TTS, basic LLMs, knowledge retrieval and tool calls. Phone calls add $0.01 per minute . A number costs $1.20 per month . New accounts get a $5 trial balance. How does Live 3 compare with other full-duplex voice models? Metrics Fish Audio Live 3 OpenAI GPT-Live-1 Eleven Realtime v1 Max Gemini 3.8 Live Design Full duplex, timing learned in the speech model Full duplex, delegates reasoning to a backend model Cascaded, tuned end to end Live dialogue model, runs tools in the background Languages English only Not disclosed 90+ 97 Published timing 186 ms minimum (short reactions) Not disclosed in post text 0.57 s avg time to first audio Not disclosed Turn-taking score Not published +30 pp Full Duplex Bench vs GPT-Realtime-2.1 (self-reported) 94.1% Full-Duplex-Bench Not disclosed Reasoning / agent score Not published #1 on Tau3 with GPT-6 Astra (medium) 98.8% Big Bench Audio; 87.1% tool tasks Extended Thinking: 97.7% Big Bench Audio; 68.6% τ-Voice Price $0.035/min promo, $0.07 list (incl. STT, basic LLM, TTS) $0.05/min voice layer + backend tokens Session time + tokens Not disclosed in launch post Deployment Agent Platform, API, on-prem API, telephony ElevenAgents, Realtime API Gemini API, AI Studio, Gemini Enterprise (preview) ElevenLabs scores come from Artificial Analysis, as reported by ElevenLabs. OpenAI and Google figures are self-reported. Key Takeaways Live 3 is Fish Audio’s full-duplex voice model for phone and web agents. It learns turn-taking from real conversations instead of silence thresholds. Short reactions can start in as little as 186 ms. Agents cost $0.035 per minute until December 31, 2026, then $0.07. English only, with no published benchmark scores yet. Check out the launch post , try it at fish.audio/live3 , and see the Agents docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. items.summary_html:
Fish Audio has released Live 3, a full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents. The Fish Audio Live 3 full-duplex voice model keeps listening while it speaks. That lets a caller pause, say “mm-hmm,” or change their mind without breaking the call. For developers, the pitch is simple. Turn-taking moves out of hand-tuned pipeline rules and into the speech model.

TL;DR
  • Product: A full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents
  • Runs on: Hosted Fish Agent Platform and Fish Audio API; on-premises for enterprises.
  • Performance: Fish Audio shows behavior demos, but publishes no benchmark scores.
  • Best: Can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms for short reactions like “mm-hmm.”
What is Fish Audio Live 3?

Live 3 is a full-duplex voice model from Fish Audio that listens and speaks at the same time.

The core argument is that speed and timing are different problems. An agent can reply fast and still speak at the wrong moment. A pause after “What time do you open?” usually ends a turn. A pause in the middle of a phone number does not.

How does Live 3 handle turn-taking?

Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and turn-taking across separate pipeline stages. Fish Audio team states that Live 3 moves conversational timing into the speech model. It was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop.

They framed the old approach as piling on “more rules and more thresholds.” Fish Audio instead wants the model to learn timing from data. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent’s instructions and tools.

The Fish Audio team walks through 3 behaviors:

  • Acknowledging without taking over. A caller reads “415… 555… 0132.” Live 3 may say “okay, 415” between chunks, then wait.
  • Telling a backchannel from an interruption. A caller saying “yeah” lets the agent continue. “Wait, actually, I just need Thursday” makes it stop.
  • Waiting through corrections. For “two pizzas… no, three,” Live 3 waits instead of logging the wrong order.
How fast is Live 3?

Fish Audio states Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms. That figure covers short reactions such as “mm-hmm,” “okay” and quick confirmations. The full answer is prepared in parallel.

This is a floor for small reactions, not time-to-first-audio for a complete reply. Fish Audio has not published a latency distribution. Third-party tracker OrcaRouter also reports no Artificial Analysis score for Live 3 as of November 11.

&

How do developers deploy Live 3?

Live 3 is available on the Fish Agent Platform, through the Fish Audio API, and on-premises for enterprises. The Agents platform is in public beta.

Agents expose a REST surface under /v1/agent/*. Browser sessions run through @fishaudio/agent-client or @fishaudio/agent-react. Agents can answer phone numbers, connect over WebRTC, or sit in a website widget. The Live 3 page lists 2,000,000+ library voices, including cloned voices.

A pending docs pull request shows Live 3 enabled with voice.engine: "live3". With it on, speech recognition is fixed to fish_audio:transcribe-stream-1. Fish Audio’s current docs say that model also classifies overlaps as interruptions or acknowledgements.

How much does Live 3 cost?

The Live 3 page lists $0.035 per minute, down 50% from $0.07, until December 31, 2026. It says the plan includes Live 3. The pricing docs say the $0.07 list rate covers STT, TTS, basic LLMs, knowledge retrieval and tool calls.

Phone calls add $0.01 per minute. A number costs $1.20 per month. New accounts get a $5 trial balance.

How does Live 3 compare with other full-duplex voice models? Key Takeaways
  • Live 3 is Fish Audio’s full-duplex voice model for phone and web agents.
  • It learns turn-taking from real conversations instead of silence thresholds.
  • Short reactions can start in as little as 186 ms.
  • Agents cost $0.035 per minute until December 31, 2026, then $0.07.
  • English only, with no published benchmark scores yet.

items.title: Australia will impose mandatory safety rules on AI. Are we focused on the right risks?
items.summary: energyy/Getty Images Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just announced six mandatory artificial intelligence (AI) safety guardrails. The government will establish a new AI safety regulator to enforce the regulations, with the power to impose significant penalties. According to the guardrails, frontier AI companies – the ones with the most powerful AI models at the cutting edge of AI development – will have to: implement security controls identify and manage serious risks allow independent evaluation of their models rapidly notify government of serious incidents publish safety and security frameworks to enhance governance and transparency respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. The implementation of the guardrails is one of 18 recommendations from a rapid review the government launched in September after an AI agent, deployed by OpenAI to collect data, accessed non-public Medicare stats . In the background, the government is pursuing an extensive agenda of technology law and policy reform. There’s a new prohibition on unfair trading practices focused on online markets, a digital duty of care bill to address harms from online platforms and AI chatbots, a significant draft privacy law reform bill , and an inquiry into Australia’s sovereign AI capability. The prime minister’s announcement focuses on “AI safety”, “AI security” and “frontier” AI models and companies. But Australians may remain unprotected from known AI harms that – though less spectacular – are already widespread and serious. A diversified approach to AI policy and regulation As well as the mandatory guardrails, the rapid review recommendations included criminal law reform, international cooperation, and strengthening mechanisms for government engagement with frontier AI developers. Nearly half of the recommendations are about increasing Australia’s preparedness for AI-related cyber incidents. The recommendations make sense. The review is right to emphasise the role of building capacity, relationships, and cooperation. Effective and responsive AI regulation must go beyond the government simply issuing and enforcing rigid rules. Despite these strengths, the government seems to be taking a narrow view of what “AI safety” means. What counts as AI safety? The announcement seems to indicate that the most important risks come from frontier AI models. But risks from AI – including serious risks to safety, public health and national security – are not confined to the frontier. AI and algorithmic systems are increasingly integrated into important services such as healthcare, insurance, housing, finance, employment, education and social security. For the most part, these kinds of AI systems are not likely to be frontier AI. Instead, these would be smaller, more specialised tools, such as an AI recruitment bot, an AI personal budgeting app or an educational grading algorithm . Unaccountable, unfair, poorly managed deployments of such everyday AI systems have the potential to cause enormous harm. We’ve seen Robodebt harm hundreds of thousands of Australians. Sexist AI-enabled job recruitment tools , AI-enabled stadium security systems that let a gun into the Melbourne Cricket Ground, racist policing algorithms , and AI meal-planners that recommend poisonous recipes are just a few among thousands of examples of everyday AI harms and risks. As the Medicare incident showed, risks also emerge from interactions between software systems, organisations and real world contexts. It doesn’t make sense to just focus on powerful AI models out of context. Worse, AI systems are notoriously opaque . While changes to privacy law will soon require businesses and government to state in their privacy policies if they use automated decision-making, Australians don’t have a right to an actual explanation of AI decisions in most domains. A lack of transparency about how (non-frontier) AI systems are developed and deployed is a serious impediment to accountability . A lighter touch The Australian government recognised all of this in an earlier 2024 proposal for mandatory AI guardrails. However, these have largely been abandoned in favour of a lighter regulatory touch. The 2024 proposal contemplated ten guardrails that would apply to non-frontier AI systems deployed in high-risk settings, as well as frontier systems. These would have included requirements for transparency, accountability, testing, data governance, record keeping, risk management, human oversight of systems, and pathways for contesting AI decisions. Most of those guardrails are missing from the new list. Now, only safety frameworks need to be transparent, for instance. Independent oversight seems limited to evaluating AI models themselves, rather than evaluating whether the development and deployment of AI systems in various contexts is safe, fair, responsible or accountable. There are also no general record-keeping or transparency guardrails that would create the paper trails we need for real oversight and accountability. Some promising changes One area that looks promising is the requirement to respond to new standards and rules. Depending on how the guardrails are implemented, standards such as Australia’s nuanced and sophisticated Voluntary AI Safety Standard could provide more detailed guidance to promote fairness, transparency and accountability. If compliance with certain standards were mandated, then guardrails could have a deeper and wider reach. Similarly, a proposal to introduce criminal liability for negligent AI developers could incentivise better record-keeping and more proactive risk management. But until the government fleshes out this bullet point list of guardrails and rapid review recommendations, it will be hard to know how broad the scope of AI safety regulation will be. For now, one thing is clear. Introducing regulation for sci-fi frontier risks such as “rogue” AI agents attacking our government or infrastructure is good politics, and sound policy. But it’s not enough to keep Australians safe from serious AI harms. Henry Fraser receives funding from the Australian Research Council through the Centre for Automated Decision-Making and Society, grant number CE200100005.

  1. implement security controls
  2. identify and manage serious risks
  3. allow independent evaluation of their models
  4. rapidly notify government of serious incidents
  5. publish safety and security frameworks to enhance governance and transparency
  6. respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

The announcement seems to indicate that the most important risks come from frontier AI models.

But risks from AI – including serious risks to safety, public health and national security – are not confined to the frontier.

A lack of transparency about how (non-frontier) AI systems are developed and deployed is a serious impediment to accountability.
